newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish troops try to trap rebel Kurds in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish troops try to trap rebel Kurds in Iraq.

text.p: Heavily armed Turkish forces tried on Sunday to trap Kurdish separatists in the border mountains of northern Iraq on the fifth day of an incursion that has been criticised by Ankara's Western allies.

F-16 jets bombed rebel positions in northern Iraqi mountains, while a column of Turkish tanks moved northeast along the road from Dohuk to the resort of Amadiya in what appeared to be preparations for a second prong of attack.

Witnesses saw 10 tanks and armoured cars at the tail of the column passing through the town of Suara Tuka early on Sunday, but local sources said around 100 tanks had passed in the direction of Bamarny and the Matin mountain, west of Amadiya.
Two helicopters circled above the convoy.

Turkish troops have been fighting rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) mainly in the Sinaht border area since they poured into the area early on Wednesday. The military has said they have killed 902 guerrillas so far for the loss of 12 members of the security forces.

Western capitals and the United Nations have criticised the operation -- being carried out under a rigorous news blackout -- urged Ankara to withdraw the troops and expressed worry for the safety of civilians.
In Baghdad on Sunday, Iraq's United Nations coordinator expressed concern over Turkey's incursion, saying it might block implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the world body.
"We are concerned about this development since it may produce an even more volatile security situation in the north, U.N. coordinator Staffan de Mistura told Reuters.
Baghdad has condemned the move as a violation of territorial integrity and a breach of international law.

Ankara said the operation was launched in response to a call from an Iraqi Kurdish group and was aimed at protecting civilians from a possible "massacre" by the PKK, which sometimes attacks Turkey from bases in northern Iraq.
"The operation is in no way aimed against the Iraqi government, other forces in the region or civilians living in northern Iraq," Foreign Ministry spokesman Omer Akbel said in a statement on Sunday.
"The operation will continue until the terrorist groups in the area are rendered ineffective and the area is controlled by (Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud) Barzani's forces," Akbel said.

Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) has been generally in charge of the border areas of northern Iraq, while a rival Kurdish group has control further south of the region, set up as an autonomous Kurdish zone by the West following the 1991 Gulf War.

KDP forces, who have in the past objected to Turkey's incursions into Iraq, have been seen working with Turkish forces and they are keeping a tight watch on journalists in the area, helping bar them from the zone and curbing communications.
"We will not allow you to travel for political reasons," said Shawkat Barmarni, a KDP official in Dohuk.
The communication and travel restrictions have made it impossible to confirm the scale of the operation or the casualty figure.

The Germany-based DEM agency, which is close to the PKK, said in a statement on Saturday that more than 40 Turkish soldiers had been killed in clashes with the rebels. It also carried a call to arms from PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan.
"I call once more to all our people to fight," DEM quoted Ocalan as telling a pro-Kurdish television channel.
Turkey's Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller was reported by Anatolian as saying she wanted the operation finished as soon as possible.
A spokesman for the anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Congress told Reuters contacts inside Arbil reported a gun battle there between members of the PKK and KDP late on Friday.
He said three PKK offices had been overrun by KDP forces, with the occupants either killed or taken prisoner by morning.
One aid organisation, the U.K.-based Mines Advisory Group, said it was pulling out of Dohuk because of security concerns.
